approachQuestion.prompt:
Badge Arrangements

A badge uses every character in a supplied string s. Return every distinct arrangement as a string, once, in any order. Equal characters are indistinguishable.

Examples:
s="aba" -> ["aab","aba","baa"].
s="xx" -> ["xx"].

Constraints: 1 <= n=s.length <= 10; lowercase English letters. Do not modify s.

options.text: Use one remaining count per letter and explore each letter with a positive count at the next position; restore the count after returning. Copy every completed path.
options.feedback: Each distinct prefix has one construction path. Restoring counts lets siblings use the same available inventory without treating equal copies as different choices.

options.text: Choose one unused occurrence index at every position and emit every completed string, without deduplication.
options.feedback: For s="aa", swapping the two occurrence identities emits "aa" twice.

options.text: Choose each distinct input character at most once in a path.
options.feedback: For s="aba", the result must contain two a characters; banning a repeated character loses all valid arrangements.

options.text: Generate all occurrence-index permutations, insert the completed strings into an ordered set, and return its keys.
options.feedback: This is correct for the entire domain, but equal letters produce redundant branches and set work that count-based choices avoid.

details: Count the 26 letters. At each position scan those 26 counts, consume one positive count, append its letter, recurse, then restore the count and path. Copy the string at length n.

Branch on available letter counts rather than indistinguishable copies of the same letter. Restore the count after each branch. This generates each distinct arrangement once without a result deduplication set.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze `acm-b18-03-search` only. Let V be the number of recursive calls including terminal calls and R the total number of characters in returned strings. Building the fixed 26-count array costs n operations. Each call scans at most 26 entries. Choose the tightest stated time and auxiliary-space pair. Count recursion and mutable working state; exclude supplied input and returned output storage, but include copying work in time. Primitive integer/index operations and preallocated-array updates cost constant time; dynamic appends are amortized constant time. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n + V + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + R) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n + V + R) time, O(V + R) auxiliary space
O(n·V + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each call scans a fixed alphabet, while emitted strings add their copied length.
details: Every call does constant bounded-alphabet work; reading s adds n and copying full strings adds R. These are all performed operations, so the stated sum is tight.
The fixed count array, n-character path, and depth-n stack use linear space.

Let V be the number of recursive calls including terminal calls and R the total number of characters in returned strings. Building the fixed 26-count array costs n operations. Each call scans at most 26 entries.
“O(n + R) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This omits the live path and stack.
“O(n + V + R) time, O(V + R) auxiliary space”: All explored prefixes are not retained, and output is excluded.
“O(n·V + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Scanning 26 counts is bounded work, not a scan of n occurrences.
